preamble: BEXS Syndrome  |  HNRNPH2-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder  |  X-Linked Syndromic Intellectual Disability, Bain Type  (OMIM 300986)

questions.domain: Age of symptom onset before 12 months?
questions.question: Yes – most individuals show signs of developmental delay before 12 months

questions.domain: Global developmental delay identified in first year of life?
questions.question: Yes – global delay across motor, language, and cognitive domains

questions.domain: Regression of acquired skills during illness or following seizures?
questions.question: Yes – ~1/3 of patients show regression followed by partial recovery

questions.domain: Previous diagnosis of Rett syndrome or atypical Rett (before genetic testing)?
questions.question: Yes – significant phenotypic overlap; HNRNPH2-NDD is a key RTT mimic

questions.domain: Hypotonia (decreased muscle tone) documented on neurological exam?
questions.question: Yes – hypotonia is nearly universal; present from early infancy

questions.domain: Significant delay in motor milestones (sitting, standing, walking)?
questions.question: Yes – motor milestones consistently delayed; some non-ambulatory

questions.domain: Gait abnormality, ataxia, or unsteady walk?
questions.question: Yes – ataxic or broad-based gait common in ambulatory patients

questions.domain: Mixed tone abnormalities (hypertonia/spasticity alongside hypotonia)?
questions.question: Yes – mixed tone picture; spasticity and hypertonia seen in subset

questions.domain: Severe language impairment – nonverbal or minimally verbal?
questions.question: Yes – severe language impairment is a hallmark major feature

questions.domain: No meaningful expressive speech by age 3?
questions.question: Yes – majority remain nonverbal or have <10 functional words at age 3

questions.domain: Absent or severely limited receptive language as well?
questions.question: Yes – both receptive and expressive language affected

questions.domain: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) or autistic-like features?
questions.question: Yes – ASD features common; some formally diagnosed with ASD

questions.domain: Stereotypic movements or hand stereotypies (wringing, mouthing)?
questions.question: Yes – hand stereotypies present; overlap with Rett syndrome behavior

questions.domain: Anxiety, self-injurious, or aggressive behavior?
questions.question: Yes – behavioral disturbances in majority; anxiety, aggression, OCD features

questions.domain: Attention difficulties consistent with ADHD features?
questions.question: Yes – inattention and hyperactivity observed in subset

questions.domain: Intellectual disability (mild to severe) on formal neurodevelopmental testing?
questions.question: Yes – intellectual disability present across spectrum, often moderate-severe

questions.domain: Seizures of any type (onset age 3–34 years reported)?
questions.question: Yes – seizures in approximately 50% of patients; variable onset age

questions.domain: Abnormal EEG findings (epileptiform discharges, abnormal background)?
questions.question: Yes – epileptiform activity on EEG in those with seizures

questions.domain: Short stature or growth restriction below expected family centile?
questions.question: Yes – growth abnormalities common; short stature frequent finding

questions.domain: Scoliosis or spinal curvature on clinical or radiographic examination?
questions.question: Yes – scoliosis common; surveillance recommended until skeletal maturity

questions.domain: Hip dysplasia confirmed on imaging?
questions.question: Yes – hip dysplasia seen especially in non-ambulatory patients

questions.domain: Joint laxity or hypermobility?
questions.question: Yes – joint laxity and ligamentous hypermobility noted in cohort

questions.domain: Pes planus (flat feet)?
questions.question: Yes – pes planus frequently documented

questions.domain: Pectus carinatum or chest wall deformity?
questions.question: Yes – pectus carinatum reported in subset of patients

questions.domain: Prominent fingertip pads?
questions.question: Yes – prominent fingertip pads are a characteristic dysmorphic feature

questions.domain: Micrognathia (small or recessed jaw)?
questions.question: Yes – micrognathia reported as recurrent dysmorphic feature

questions.domain: Shortened palpebral fissures or concave/arched eyebrows?
questions.question: Yes – shortened palpebral fissures and concave eyebrows described

questions.domain: Feeding difficulties or failure to thrive in infancy?
questions.question: Yes – feeding problems common; many require G-tube or NG tube

questions.domain: Chronic constipation?
questions.question: Yes – constipation is a consistent GI complaint across the cohort

questions.domain: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)?
questions.question: Yes – GERD documented in multiple patients

questions.domain: Dysphagia or swallowing difficulties?
questions.question: Yes – dysphagia present; some require videofluoroscopic swallow study

questions.domain: Strabismus (crossed eyes or ocular misalignment)?
questions.question: Yes – strabismus present in majority of those with visual involvement (~75%)

questions.domain: Cortical visual impairment (CVI)?
questions.question: Yes – CVI present in subset; requires ophthalmologic evaluation

questions.domain: Sensory processing disorder or sensory hypersensitivity?
questions.question: Yes – sensory processing difficulties frequently reported by caregivers

questions.domain: Sleep disturbance or suspected sleep apnea?
questions.question: Yes – sleep disturbances common; sleep study may be warranted

questions.domain: Brain MRI: cerebellar abnormalities (vermis hypoplasia, cerebellar hypoplasia)?
questions.question: Yes – cerebellar anomalies documented (vermis hypoplasia in subset)

questions.domain: Brain MRI: cortical abnormalities, white matter signal changes, or thin corpus callosum?
questions.question: Variable – cortical and white matter abnormalities in minority of patients

questions.domain: Confirmed de novo mutation (unaffected parents, no family history)?
questions.question: Yes – >95% of pathogenic HNRNPH2 variants arise de novo

questions.domain: Female sex at birth (historically higher phenotypic identification)?
questions.question: Yes – initially identified predominantly in females; male cases now confirmed

questions.domain: No family history of similar neurodevelopmental disorder?
questions.question: Yes – sporadic occurrence; negative family history typical for de novo

questions.domain: Pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in HNRNPH2 (Xq22.1) identified?
questions.question: Yes – heterozygous (females) or hemizygous (males) HNRNPH2 variant confirmed

questions.domain: Variant located within or adjacent to nuclear localization signal (NLS/PY-NLS)?
questions.question: Yes – NLS variants (e.g., R206W, R206G, P209L) most common and most severe

questions.domain: De novo origin confirmed by parental trio exome/genome sequencing?
questions.question: Yes – trio testing confirms de novo mutation; not inherited from either parent

questions.domain: Variant predicted to disrupt Kapβ2 (karyopherin β2) nuclear transport interaction?
questions.question: Yes – NLS mutations reduce Kapβ2 binding, causing cytoplasmic protein mislocation

questions.domain: No pathogenic MECP2 variant (excludes classic Rett syndrome)?
questions.question: Yes – MECP2 negative; HNRNPH2-NDD is a key RTT phenocopy

questions.domain: No pathogenic FOXG1 or CDKL5 variant (excludes atypical Rett)?
questions.question: Yes – negative for atypical RTT genes; further supports HNRNPH2 diagnosis

questions.domain: No pathogenic ANKRD11 variant (excludes KBG syndrome)?
questions.question: Yes – KBG syndrome shares dysmorphic and ID features; excluded

questions.domain: No features of Angelman syndrome (normal UBE3A/chromosome 15)?
questions.question: Yes – Angelman excluded; normal methylation and UBE3A on 15q11-q13

questions.domain: No pathogenic HNRNPH1 variant (close paralog, overlapping phenotype)?
questions.question: Yes – HNRNPH1-related NDD is the closest mimic; excluded by sequencing

sections.heading:
Clinical History: No additional cost (obtained during patient encounter and caregiver interview)
Clinical Assessment: $200–500 (formal developmental/psychological/behavioral evaluation — e.g., ADOS-2, Vineland)
Clinical Exam: No additional cost (physical and dysmorphology examination by clinician)
Medium: $300–1,500 (EEG, plain radiographs for scoliosis/hips, ophthalmology visit, modified barium swallow)
Large: $3,000–15,000+ (brain MRI with sedation, clinical exome sequencing trio, functional variant studies)

Pathogenic HNRNPH2 variant identified (25 points) — DEFINITIVE
Variant in nuclear localization signal/PY-NLS region (15 points) — PATHOGNOMONIC LOCATION
De novo origin confirmed by trio sequencing (8 points) — CONFIRMATORY
Global developmental delay (10 points) — ESSENTIAL MAJOR FEATURE
Severe language impairment/nonverbal (10 points) — ESSENTIAL MAJOR FEATURE
Hypotonia (8 points) — NEARLY UNIVERSAL FINDING
Delayed motor milestones (8 points) — MAJOR FEATURE
Intellectual disability on formal testing (8 points) — MAJOR FEATURE
Seizures in ~50% of patients (8 points) — SIGNIFICANT MINOR FEATURE
Symptom onset before 12 months (8 points) — CRITICAL EARLY RED FLAG

Phase 1 — Clinical Evaluation (No/Low Cost):
  • Comprehensive developmental history and caregiver interview
  • Full neurological and dysmorphology physical examination
  • Developmental milestone review and early regression timeline
  • Behavioral assessment (ASD screening, ADHD features, stereotypies)
  Potential: 50–70 points for $0–500

Phase 2 — Targeted Investigations ($300–1,500):
  • EEG if seizures suspected or confirmed
  • Formal neurodevelopmental/psychological testing (ADOS-2, Vineland, IQ)
  • Ophthalmologic evaluation (strabismus, CVI)
  • Skeletal X-rays for scoliosis and hip dysplasia surveillance
  Additional: 10–20 points for $500–1,500

Phase 3 — Definitive Genetic Testing ($3,000–15,000+):
  • Clinical whole exome sequencing (WES) — proband + parent trio preferred
  • If WES nondiagnostic: whole genome sequencing (WGS)
  • Brain MRI with sedation for neuroimaging characterization
  • Functional variant studies if variant of uncertain significance (VUS) found
  Additional: 40–55 points — crossing diagnostic threshold

• GENETIC TESTING IS REQUIRED for definitive diagnosis — no clinical biomarker or imaging finding is pathognomonic without a confirmed HNRNPH2 pathogenic variant
• Ultra-rare disease: as of 2025, approximately 67 individuals identified worldwide; high index of suspicion required in any child with unexplained global DD + hypotonia + severe language impairment
• BEXS (Bain type X-linked syndromic) is the eponymous name; also referred to as HNRNPH2-NDD (OMIM 300986)
• X-linked condition (Xq22.1): affects females (heterozygous) and males (hemizygous); males with NLS variants tend to have more severe phenotype
• >90% of pathogenic variants are missense mutations within or adjacent to the nuclear localization signal (PY-NLS); R206W and R206G are the most recurrent variants
• Rett Syndrome overlap: HNRNPH2-NDD should be included in the RTT/atypical RTT differential — 12 of 26 patients in one cohort met criteria for atypical RTT
• Surveillance at every visit: growth parameters, feeding safety, seizure review, developmental progress, behavioral status, scoliosis, sleep disturbance
• No disease-modifying treatment exists; management is supportive (PT, OT, speech therapy, anti-seizure medications, GI management, orthopedic care)
• Genetic counseling essential: de novo in most cases means low recurrence risk (<1%), but germline mosaicism has been documented

NLS/PY-NLS Variants (e.g., R206W, R206G, P209L) — Most Severe:
  • Profound intellectual disability, minimal or absent speech, severe motor impairment
  • Highest seizure burden; more likely to require wheelchair and G-tube
  • Males with NLS variants: very severe to potentially lethal phenotype

Non-NLS Missense Variants — Milder Spectrum:
  • Mild developmental delay, autistic features, psychiatric diagnoses
  • Males with non-NLS variants (e.g., R29C, nonsense/frameshift): mild DD + autism

HNRNPH1 Paralogue: Variants in HNRNPH1 produce nearly identical clinical phenotype — distinguish only by sequencing

Differential Diagnoses to Exclude:
  • Classic Rett Syndrome (MECP2) — most important mimic
  • Atypical Rett (FOXG1, CDKL5)
  • Angelman Syndrome (UBE3A, 15q11-q13)
  • KBG Syndrome (ANKRD11)
  • HNRNPH1-related NDD
  • Other X-linked intellectual disability syndromes

confidenceNote:
🔴  85–100 points: High Confidence — BEXS Syndrome/HNRNPH2-NDD highly likely; genetic confirmation required; proceed to HNRNPH2 sequencing (trio WES preferred)
🟡  40–84 points: Moderate Confidence — HNRNPH2-NDD probable or possible; whole exome sequencing strongly indicated; clinical genetics referral
🟢  <40 points: Low Confidence — HNRNPH2-NDD less likely; broaden differential to other X-linked or autosomal neurodevelopmental disorders
